newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian PM to talk to Clinton about condemned man.
newsitem.headline: Italian PM to talk to Clinton about condemned man.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi will tell U.S. President Bill Clinton at the Denver summit of his concern about a U.S. decision to uphold the death sentence on a convicted murderer, a junior minister said on Friday.
Joseph O'Dell was condemned to death in 1985 after being found guilty of killing a woman, but supporters say DNA testing proves he did not carry out the crime.

The state of Virginia scheduled his execution for last December but the U.S. Supreme Court blocked the sentence at the last minute after worldwide protests, especially from Italy, where Pope John Paul and Prodi made pleas for clemency.
However the Supreme Court on Thursday rejected the convicted murderer's claims that his death sentence should be overturned and said his execution could go ahead as before.
Foreign ministry undersecretary Piero Fassino told parliament he would contact Prodi, who is in Denver for a Group of Seven summit, to inform him of the ruling.
"Thereby he can tell President Clinton directly about the worries and position of the Italian government and parliament," Fassino said.
The speaker of the Italian upper house of parliament, Nicola Mancino, said he had sent a letter to the Governor of Virginia, George Allen, asking him to commute O'Dell's death sentence.
The Supreme Court ruling did not consider O'Dell's guilt or innocence, only whether he should receive the death penalty or should be resentenced to life in prison.
The court, by a 5-4 vote, rejected claims that the death sentence should be overturned because he was not allowed to tell his jury that an alternative to death was life without parole.
Hands off Cain, an anti-death penalty group which staged street protests in Rome last December against O'Dell's death sentence, described the high court ruling as "a vendetta".

"It can only be explained as an act of spite against the great mobilisation, especially by Italians and the Pope, which six months ago forced it to suspend the death sentence a few hours before the execution," the group said in a statement.

Although the U.S. court cleared the way for his execution, O'Dell can appeal to Virginia governor Allen for clemency. Allen had said he would wait for the high court ruling before deciding whether O'Dell should die by lethal injection.
